title: Cartan Subalgebras and Root Space Decompositions

items.title: The additive Jordan–Chevalley supplier
items.statement: The operator theorem used here is [[thm-additive-jordan-chevalley-decomposition]]. Its published contract assumes the Axiom of Choice; this page invokes that contract only for finite-dimensional complex endomorphisms and records the assumption at the first proof-bearing use.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Jordan–Chevalley parts under the adjoint representation
items.statement: The compatibility of abstract and operator Jordan–Chevalley parts is proof-bearing, so it is supplied by the subsequent lemma rather than imported as an unproved convention.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Abstract Jordan decomposition
items.statement: An element x of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra has an abstract Jordan decomposition if x=x_s+x_n, [x_s,x_n]=0, and ad(x_s) is semisimple while ad(x_n) is nilpotent. Existence and uniqueness for complex semisimple Lie algebras are proved below.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II
Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Jordan–Chevalley parts agree under the adjoint representation
items.statement: Assume AC. If x=x_s+x_n is an abstract Jordan decomposition in a complex semisimple Lie algebra, then ad(x)_s=ad(x_s) and ad(x)_n=ad(x_n); conversely the unique inner derivations giving the additive Jordan–Chevalley parts of ad(x) determine x_s and x_n.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: For an existing abstract decomposition, uniqueness of the commuting semisimple-plus-nilpotent operator split identifies ad(x_s) and ad(x_n) with the additive Jordan–Chevalley parts. Conversely apply the published polynomial construction to ad(x): generalized eigenspaces multiply under brackets, so both polynomial parts are derivations; innerness writes them as ad(y_s), ad(y_n), and centerlessness transfers their sum, commutation, semisimplicity, nilpotence, and uniqueness to y_s,y_n. AC is used only through the published additive Jordan–Chevalley theorem.

items.title: Jordan decomposition lies inside a complex semisimple Lie algebra
items.statement: Assume AC. Every element x of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra has a unique abstract Jordan decomposition x=x_s+x_n, and ad(x_s), ad(x_n) are the additive Jordan–Chevalley parts of ad(x).

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Decompose ad(x) by the cited operator theorem. Prove its polynomial parts are derivations by decomposing g into generalized eigenspaces and checking brackets add eigenvalues. Innerness produces x_s,x_n; centerlessness transfers sum and commutation from adjoints to elements. Uniqueness follows from uniqueness of the operator split. AC is used only through the published operator theorem.

items.title: Normalizer of a Lie subalgebra
items.statement: For a subalgebra h of g, N_g(h)={x in g:[x,h] is contained in h}. It is a Lie subalgebra and contains h.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Cartan subalgebra
items.statement: A Cartan subalgebra of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra is a nilpotent subalgebra h satisfying N_g(h)=h. This definition is valid beyond the semisimple complex case.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Toral and maximal toral subalgebras
items.statement: A toral subalgebra of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra is an abelian subalgebra all of whose adjoint endomorphisms are semisimple. It is maximal toral if it is maximal by inclusion among toral subalgebras.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Regular element and rank
items.statement: For finite-dimensional complex g, x is regular if dim ker(ad x) is minimal among all elements; that minimum is rank(g). A regular semisimple element is regular and has semisimple adjoint.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Centralizer of a regular semisimple element is Cartan
items.statement: If g is complex semisimple and x is regular semisimple, then g^x=ker(ad x) is a Cartan subalgebra.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Diagonalize ad(x), so its zero eigenspace is g^x and brackets respect eigenvalue addition. If y normalizes g^x, its nonzero eigencomponents would send x to corresponding nonzero eigenspaces, contradicting normalization, hence y lies in g^x. For z in g^x, vary x+t z: minimal kernel dimension forces ad(z)|g^x nilpotent; Engel makes g^x nilpotent. Thus it is self-normalizing and Cartan.

items.title: Existence of Cartan subalgebras
items.statement: Assume AC. Every finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra has a Cartan subalgebra.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: The zero algebra has Cartan subalgebra zero. Otherwise Engel and the internal Jordan decomposition produce a nonzero semisimple element, so finite dimension gives a toral subalgebra t maximal by dimension. Simultaneously diagonalize ad(t) and put l=C_g(t), the zero weight space. Killing invariance pairs only opposite t-weights; Cartan's semisimplicity criterion therefore makes B_g|l nondegenerate. For x in l, polynomial functoriality puts its Jordan parts x_s,x_n in l, and maximality of t forces x_s in t. Hence ad_l(x)=ad_l(x_n) is nilpotent, so Engel makes l nilpotent. Lie triangularization of l on g makes [l,l] strictly upper triangular, giving B_g([l,l],l)=0; nondegeneracy forces l abelian. Now ad(x_n) commutes with ad(l), so every product ad(x_n)ad(y), y in l, is nilpotent and has trace zero. Thus x_n is B_g-orthogonal to l and vanishes. Every element of l is therefore semisimple, so l is toral and maximality gives l=t. The joint-weight calculation then gives N_g(t)=C_g(t)=t; hence t is Cartan. AC is used only through the published Jordan–Chevalley supplier.

items.title: Generalized weight spaces of a nilpotent subalgebra
items.statement: For a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra g and a nilpotent subalgebra h, the generalized weight spaces g_alpha form a direct sum decomposition of g, are h-stable, contain h in g_0, and satisfy [g_alpha,g_beta] contained in g_{alpha+beta}.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Simultaneous generalized eigenspace refinement: invariance under ad h by the displayed commutator identity and the induction over the nilpotent filtration of h, then Lie's theorem on each intersection to identify the weight functionals, and the binomial expansion for the bracket inclusion.

items.title: Cartan subalgebras are exactly maximal toral subalgebras
items.statement: Assume AC. In a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra, the Cartan subalgebras are precisely the maximal toral subalgebras.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: For a Cartan h, Lie triangularization and nilpotence show all nilpotent parts of its elements lie in the common zero-weight ideal; semisimplicity and self-normalization force those parts to vanish and h to be abelian, hence toral. Its centralizer equals h, so it is maximal. Conversely a maximal toral t is the zero-weight space for ad(t); regular elements of t have this centralizer, and the normalizer calculation plus Engel gives N_g(t)=t. AC is used only through the internal Jordan decomposition and Cartan-existence suppliers.

items.title: Conjugacy of Cartan subalgebras
items.statement: Assume AC. Any two Cartan subalgebras of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra are carried to one another by an inner automorphism in the connected adjoint group.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Let G be the connected subgroup generated by exp(ad y). On G×h_reg, (g,x)↦g·x has surjective differential because g=[g,x]+h for regular x. Its image is therefore open in the regular semisimple locus. Repeat for every Cartan. The complement of the discriminant in the complex vector space g is connected (intersect a generic complex line and detour finitely many points), so these disjoint open conjugacy classes form one class. Centralizers then conjugate. AC is inherited through the preceding Cartan/maximal-toral equivalence.

items.title: Root and root space
items.statement: For a Cartan subalgebra h of complex semisimple g and α in h*, define g_α={x:[H,x]=α(H)x for all H in h}. A root is a nonzero α with g_α nonzero; Φ(g,h) denotes the set of roots.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Root-space decomposition
items.statement: Assume AC. For a Cartan subalgebra h of complex semisimple g, g=h direct-sum ⊕_{α∈Φ} g_α, where Φ is finite and the zero common eigenspace is h.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The commuting family ad(H), H∈h, is simultaneously diagonalizable, giving finitely many joint weights. The zero space is the centralizer C_g(h); maximal torality plus Jordan decomposition shows C_g(h)=h. Collect the nonzero joint weight spaces. AC is inherited only through the Cartan/maximal-toral and Jordan-decomposition suppliers.

items.title: Brackets of root spaces
items.statement: For weights α,β (allowing zero), [g_α,g_β] is contained in g_{α+β}; if α+β is neither zero nor a root, the bracket is zero.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: For H∈h apply Jacobi: [H,[x,y]]=[[H,x],y]+[x,[H,y]]=(α+β)(H)[x,y]. This puts every bracket in the asserted joint eigenspace.

items.title: Killing-form orthogonality of root spaces
items.statement: If α+β≠0 then the Killing form B pairs g_α and g_β to zero. It restricts nondegenerately to h and pairs g_α only with g_{-α}.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Invariance gives (α(H)+β(H))B(x,y)=0; choose H separating α+β from zero. Since B is nondegenerate on semisimple g, the root decomposition then forces perfect pairings between opposite spaces and nondegeneracy on h.

items.title: Opposite root spaces pair nondegenerately
items.statement: For every root α, -α is a root and B:g_α×g_{-α}→C is a nondegenerate pairing.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: A nonzero x∈g_α cannot be orthogonal to all of g. Orthogonality leaves only g_{-α}; hence that space exists and the induced pairing has zero left and right radicals.

items.title: Killing-dual vector of a root
items.statement: Because B|h is nondegenerate, t_α∈h is the unique vector satisfying B(t_α,H)=α(H) for every H∈h.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Bracket of opposite root spaces
items.statement: For x∈g_α and y∈g_{-α}, [x,y]=B(x,y)t_α. Consequently [g_α,g_{-α}]=C t_α.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: For H∈h, invariance gives B([x,y],H)=B(x,[y,H])=α(H)B(x,y). Nondegeneracy on h identifies [x,y] with B(x,y)t_α; the perfect opposite pairing makes the image nonzero.

items.title: The Killing length of a root is nonzero
items.statement: For every root α of a complex semisimple Lie algebra, B(t_α,t_α)=α(t_α) is nonzero.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: If α(t_α)=0, choose paired x∈g_α,y∈g_{-α}. The span of x,y,t_α is solvable, with t_α a nonzero element of its derived algebra. Lie triangularization of its adjoint action on g makes ad(t_α) nilpotent. But t_α lies in the toral Cartan, so ad(t_α) is also semisimple; it must vanish. Centerlessness then gives t_α=0, contradicting its Killing-dual definition.

items.title: Coroot of a Lie-algebra root
items.statement: For α∈Φ define h_α=2t_α/B(t_α,t_α). Then α(h_α)=2.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: The special linear Lie algebra sl_2
items.statement: sl_2(C) is the three-dimensional Lie algebra of traceless complex two-by-two matrices under the commutator, with basis e, f, h satisfying [h,e]=2e, [h,f]=-2f, [e,f]=h.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Definition by the standard matrix model and its bracket table.

items.title: Root sl₂ triple
items.statement: For every root α there are e_α∈g_α and f_α∈g_{-α} with [e_α,f_α]=h_α, [h_α,e_α]=2e_α, and [h_α,f_α]=-2f_α; their span is isomorphic to sl₂(C).

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Choose nonzero e and use the perfect pairing to scale f so B(e,f)=2/B(t_α,t_α). The opposite-bracket formula yields h_α, while membership in the root spaces gives the other two relations. Linear independence and the standard brackets identify sl₂.

items.title: Finite-dimensional representations of sl₂
items.statement: Every finite-dimensional complex sl₂-module is a direct sum of irreducibles V(n), n≥0. In V(n), h has weights n,n-2,…,-n, each once, and e,f move adjacent weight spaces with the standard nonzero coefficients.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Compute the Killing form of sl₂ to see it is semisimple, then invoke complete reducibility. In an irreducible module choose a maximal h-weight killed by e; the identities [e,f^k]=k f^{k-1}(h-k+1) show its weight is a nonnegative integer, produce exactly the displayed string, and irreducibility makes it the whole module.

items.title: Root-string property
items.statement: For a root α and β either a root or zero, the nonzero spaces g_{β+kα} occur for an unbroken interval -p≤k≤q and satisfy p-q=β(h_α)∈Z.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Restrict the adjoint representation to the root sl₂. Each irreducible summand contributes a consecutive interval of indices centred at -β(h_α)/2; their union is a nested interval containing zero, and its endpoints give p-q=β(h_α).

items.title: Cartan integers are integral
items.statement: For all roots α,β, the Cartan integer ⟨β,α∨⟩=β(h_α)=2(β,α)/(α,α) is an integer.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: For nonproportional roots this is p-q. For proportional roots, apply the sl₂ weight calculation directly; the subsequent reducedness theorem identifies the only nonzero cases as ±2.

items.title: Root spaces are one-dimensional
items.statement: Each root space g_α of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra has dimension one.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Restrict the proportional-root subalgebra h⊕Σ_{k≠0}g_{kα} to the root sl₂. Its zero-weight space is h, and ker(α)⊂h consists of trivial modules, leaving only the one-dimensional line Ch_α available as the zero-weight line of nontrivial irreducibles. Thus exactly one nontrivial irreducible occurs. It contains e_α of weight 2, so it is V(2); consequently its weight-2 space g_α is one-dimensional (and simultaneously there are no roots kα with |k|>1).

items.title: Root systems are reduced
items.statement: If α is a root and cα is a root for c∈C, then c=±1.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Both c and 1/c give integral Cartan integers, forcing c∈{±1,±2,±1/2}. A trace-of-commutator computation on the negative-multiple root spaces proves locally that no doubled root exists, excluding the four doubled alternatives.

items.title: Root reflection
items.statement: For α∈Φ define s_α on h* by s_α(λ)=λ-λ(h_α)α. It fixes ker α and sends α to -α.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Root reflections preserve roots
items.statement: For every α∈Φ, s_α permutes Φ.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The α-string through β has endpoints β-pα and β+qα with p-q=β(h_α). Reflection sends β+kα to β-(β(h_α)+k)α and reverses this finite string, hence maps every root to a root.

items.title: Root reflections are inner
items.statement: The automorphism exp(ad e_α) exp(ad(-f_α)) exp(ad e_α) normalizes h and induces s_α on h* (up to the equivalent inverse convention).

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The adjoint root operators are nilpotent, so the exponentials are finite sums and inner automorphisms. Direct computation in each finite sl₂-string sends its weight k space to weight -k; on h it sends H to H-α(H)h_α. Dualizing gives s_α.

items.title: Lie-algebra roots form a reduced crystallographic root system
items.statement: Assume AC through the Cartan and Jordan–Chevalley construction. The real span E of Φ admits a positive-definite inner product for which Φ is a finite spanning reduced crystallographic root system: it is reflection-stable, has integral Cartan integers, and contains only ±α on each root line.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The reflections permute the finite spanning set Φ, so their faithful action makes the generated group finite. Average any auxiliary Euclidean form over this finite group. For each s_α, its fixed hyperplane is orthogonal to its (-1)-eigenline Rα in the averaged form, so the reflection formula forces its coefficient to be 2(β,α)/(α,α)=β(h_α). The cited results give integrality, reflection invariance, and reducedness; finiteness and spanning hold by construction. AC is inherited through the root-space and Cartan/Jordan–Chevalley chain, not used by the finite averaging step.

items.title: Dimension formula from roots
items.statement: For complex semisimple g with Cartan h and root system Φ, dim g=dim h+|Φ|=rank(g)+|Φ|.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Take dimensions in the direct root-space decomposition and use one-dimensionality for every root summand.

items.title: Center as the common root kernel
items.statement: For a reductive complex Lie algebra with toral h and root decomposition, Z(g)∩h=⋂_{α∈Φ}ker α; in the semisimple case this intersection is zero.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: An H∈h commutes with h and acts on g_α by α(H), so it is central exactly when every root vanishes on it. Semisimple g is centerless.

items.title: Regular root hyperplanes
items.statement: Inside a Cartan h set h_reg=h minus the union of the hyperplanes ker α over α∈Φ; its complement consists of singular Cartan elements.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.title: Centralizer dimension from vanishing roots
items.statement: For H∈h, g^H=h direct-sum ⊕_{α(H)=0}g_α, hence dim g^H=dim h+#{α:α(H)=0}.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: On g_α the map ad(H) is scalar multiplication by α(H), while it vanishes on h. Its kernel is exactly the displayed direct sum; take dimensions.

items.title: Regular Cartan elements are dense Zariski open
items.statement: The regular elements of h are h_reg, the complement of finitely many root hyperplanes; it is nonempty Zariski open and dense.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The product of the finitely many nonzero linear forms α is a nonzero polynomial. Its nonvanishing locus is h_reg. The centralizer formula gives its minimum dimension dim h exactly there.

items.title: A Cartan subalgebra is always maximal abelian
items.statement: False: in an arbitrary Lie algebra, being maximal abelian is not equivalent to being nilpotent and self-normalizing.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Refute with the two-dimensional nonabelian algebra [x,y]=y: Cy is a maximal abelian ideal but its normalizer is all of g, whereas Cx is self-normalizing.

items.title: Every element of a complex semisimple Lie algebra is semisimple
items.statement: False: semisimplicity of the Lie algebra does not make every adjoint endomorphism semisimple.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: In sl₂ the root vector e is nonzero and ad(e) is nilpotent, so e is a nilpotent rather than semisimple element.

items.title: Root spaces may have arbitrary dimension
items.statement: False: relative to a Cartan subalgebra of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra every root space is one-dimensional.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The cited theorem proves dimension one; sl₂ also exhibits the sharp value.

items.title: Sums of roots are always roots
items.statement: False: α+β need not be a root even when α and β are roots.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Take β=α in the reduced root system of sl₂: α is a root but 2α is not.

items.title: All integer multiples of a root are roots
items.statement: False: a reduced root system contains only α and -α on the line through α.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The reducedness corollary excludes 2α, already in the root system of sl₂.

items.title: Complex root data classify real semisimple Lie algebras without extra data
items.statement: False: the complex root system forgets the real form.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The real algebras sl₂(R) and su(2) are nonisomorphic (their Killing forms have different signatures) but have isomorphic complexification sl₂(C) and hence the same complex root system.

items.title: Diagonal Cartan subalgebra and roots of sl_n
items.statement: For n≥2 the diagonal traceless subalgebra h of sl_n(C) is a Cartan subalgebra, the roots are the functionals ε_i−ε_j with i≠j, and the root spaces are the lines C E_ij; so Φ has n(n−1) elements.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Compute [H,E_ij]=(ε_i−ε_j)(H)E_ij for diagonal H, verify the diagonal is maximal toral and self-normalising, and count the n(n−1) roots.

title: Cartan Subalgebras and Root Space Decompositions — Examples

items.title: The Cartan subalgebra and roots of sl₂
items.statement: For h=C·diag(1,-1) in sl₂, the roots are ±α with α(h)=2 and root spaces Ce and Cf.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Compute the three commutators with h, check h is maximal toral, and identify the zero and nonzero eigenspaces.

items.title: Root-space brackets for matrix units
items.statement: In slₙ, [E_ij,E_kl]=δ_jk E_il-δ_li E_kj realizes addition of roots whenever the sum is a root.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Multiply matrix units explicitly and compare ε_i-ε_j+ε_k-ε_l with the nonzero terms.

items.title: Cartan subalgebras of a direct sum
items.statement: If h_i is Cartan in semisimple g_i, then h_1⊕h_2 is Cartan in g_1⊕g_2 and the roots are the two root systems embedded in the dual direct sum.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Compute the normalizer componentwise and decompose each summand; no mixed roots occur.

items.title: A root sl₂ triple inside slₙ
items.statement: For α=ε_i-ε_j in slₙ, E_ij,E_ji,E_ii-E_jj form its root sl₂ triple.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Direct matrix multiplication gives the three sl₂ brackets and α(E_ii-E_jj)=2.

items.title: Root strings in type A₂
items.statement: For A₂ with simple roots α,β, the α-string through β is {β,β+α}, so p=0,q=1 and β(h_α)=-1.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: List the six A₂ roots and verify the endpoints and Cartan integer.

items.title: B₂ and C₂ from matrix Lie algebras
items.statement: The standard Cartans of so₅(C) and sp₄(C) yield coordinate root sets B₂={±e_i,±e_1±e_2} and C₂={±2e_i,±e_1±e_2}; after rescaling and swapping long and short roots these root systems are isomorphic.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Use diagonal blocks to compute the adjoint weights of the defining matrix entries, then give the explicit orthogonal similarity exchanging the two octagons.

items.title: Regular and singular diagonal elements of slₙ
items.statement: A traceless diagonal H=diag(t_i) is regular exactly when the t_i are pairwise distinct; each equality t_i=t_j contributes the corresponding root spaces to its centralizer.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Evaluate every root ε_i-ε_j on H and apply the centralizer formula.

items.title: A maximal abelian subalgebra need not be Cartan
items.statement: In the two-dimensional algebra [x,y]=y, Cy is maximal abelian but is not Cartan.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Every element outside Cy has nonzero x-component and fails to commute with y, so Cy is maximal abelian; it is an ideal, so its normalizer is all of g and it is not self-normalizing.

items.title: The Weyl reflection in sl₂
items.statement: For the standard sl₂ triple, exp(ad e)exp(ad(-f))exp(ad e) sends h to -h and interchanges the two root spaces up to sign.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Evaluate the three finite exponential series on e,f,h and compare with s_α.

items.title: Killing form and coroot directions
items.statement: In slₙ the Killing form is B(X,Y)=2n tr(XY); for α=ε_i-ε_j, its dual vector is (E_ii-E_jj)/(2n) and h_α=E_ii-E_jj.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Compute traces against a traceless diagonal H, then normalize so α(h_α)=2.

title: Root Systems Dynkin Diagrams and Cartan Killing Classification

items.title: Reduced crystallographic Euclidean root system
items.statement: A reduced crystallographic root system is a finite spanning subset Φ of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space E, excluding zero, such that s_α(Φ)=Φ, 2(β,α)/(α,α) is integral for all roots, and Rα∩Φ={±α}.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Rank and isomorphism of root systems
items.statement: The rank is dim E. An isomorphism Φ→Φ′ is a linear isomorphism E→E′ carrying Φ onto Φ′ and preserving all Cartan integers; equivalently it preserves angles and common scale on each irreducible component.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Coroot and dual root system
items.statement: For α∈Φ set α∨=2α/(α,α). The dual root system is Φ∨={α∨:α∈Φ} in E.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Weyl group
items.statement: The Weyl group W(Φ) is the subgroup of O(E) generated by the root reflections s_α(x)=x-(x,α∨)α.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: The Weyl group is finite and faithful
items.statement: W(Φ) is finite and its permutation action on Φ is faithful.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Each generator permutes the finite set Φ, giving W→Sym(Φ). If an element fixes every root, it fixes their span E, hence is the identity; thus the map is injective and W is finite.

items.title: Reducible and irreducible root systems
items.statement: Φ is reducible if E=E₁ orthogonal-direct-sum E₂ with both nonzero and Φ=(Φ∩E₁) disjoint-union (Φ∩E₂); otherwise it is irreducible.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Unique irreducible decomposition
items.statement: Every root system is the orthogonal disjoint union of irreducible root systems, uniquely up to order.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Join two roots when their inner product is nonzero and take connected components. Roots in different components are orthogonal; each component spans an orthogonal subspace and is irreducible because any orthogonal split would disconnect its graph. Connectivity makes the components intrinsic.

items.title: Rank-two root-system classification
items.statement: For two nonproportional roots the Cartan-integer product is 0, 1, 2, or 3. Their angle is respectively 90°, 60° or 120°, 45° or 135°, or 30° or 150°, with the corresponding length ratio. For a rank-two base the angle is nonacute, so the possibilities are 90°, 120°, 135°, and 150°. Thus the irreducible reduced crystallographic rank-two systems are A₂, B₂(=C₂), and G₂, while the reducible case is A₁×A₁.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: For nonproportional α,β multiply the two Cartan integers to get 4cos²θ, a nonnegative integer below 4. This gives 0,1,2,3 and both the acute and obtuse supplementary angle possibilities. For a simple pair, the nonpositive-inner-product argument selects the nonacute representative. Reflection closure generates the four finite configurations; reducedness rules out extra collinear roots and the ordered Cartan integers fix the length ratio.

items.title: Positive systems and simple roots
items.statement: Choose regular v∈E. Put Φ⁺={α:(v,α)>0}; a positive root is simple if it is not a sum of two positive roots, and Δ denotes the associated set of simple roots. The following theorem proves that Δ is a basis.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Simple roots form a signed integral basis
items.statement: The simple roots Δ form a basis of E, and every root is an integral combination of Δ whose nonzero coefficients are all nonnegative or all nonpositive.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Induct on (v,α) among positive roots: a nonsimple root splits into two smaller positive roots, yielding nonnegative integral coordinates. If simple roots had a real dependence, separate positive and negative coefficients; pair the two equal positive combinations and use that distinct simple roots have nonpositive inner product (proved by the rank-two alternatives) to force both sides zero. Thus Δ is independent and spans because Φ spans E.

items.title: Distinct simple roots have nonpositive inner product
items.statement: If α and β are distinct simple roots, then (α,β)≤0, and α-β is not a root.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: If their inner product were positive, the rank-two root-string alternatives make α-β a root; whichever sign it has expresses one simple root as a sum of positive roots, contradiction. The same reasoning excludes α-β directly.

items.title: Height and highest root
items.statement: For β=Σ n_iα_i in a chosen base, ht(β)=Σn_i. Define the root order by β≤γ when γ-β is a nonnegative integral sum of simple roots. A maximal positive root in this order is called a highest root; existence and uniqueness in the irreducible case are proved next.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Existence and uniqueness of the highest root
items.statement: Every irreducible reduced crystallographic finite root system has a unique highest root relative to each chosen base.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

source_locators: Chapter II, Problems 7–8, printed p. 204: positive-root chains and largest-root dominance; uniqueness is completed by the local finite root-order argument
items.strategy: Finiteness gives a maximal positive root theta. If (theta,alpha_i)<0 for a simple root, the rank-two alternatives force theta+alpha_i to be a root, contradicting maximality; hence theta is dominant. Connectedness also forces theta to have full simple-root support: a first vertex just outside its support would again pair negatively and could be added. If theta and theta' were two maximal positive roots, both have full support, so dominance gives (theta,theta')>0 unless they coincide. The rank-two alternatives then make theta-theta' a root; signed simple-root coordinates make one of its two signs positive, so one maximal root strictly dominates the other, a contradiction. Reducedness handles the proportional case.

items.title: Root, coroot, weight, and coweight lattices
items.statement: Q=ΣZα, Q∨=ΣZα∨, P={λ:(λ,α∨)∈Z for all α}, and P∨={μ:(α,μ)∈Z for all α}.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Fundamental weights
items.statement: For a base Δ={α_i}, the fundamental weights ω_i are the vectors dual to the simple coroots: (ω_i,α_j∨)=δ_ij.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Open and closed Weyl chambers
items.statement: The root hyperplanes divide E into open chambers. The fundamental chamber is C={x:(x,α_i)>0}; its closure replaces > by ≥.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Simple transitivity on Weyl chambers
items.statement: The Weyl group acts simply transitively on the open Weyl chambers.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: First lower the height of a positive root by simple reflections until it is simple; conjugating its reflection proves that the simple reflections generate W. Reflect a regular point across a simple wall whenever a positive root has negative pairing; the number of sign disagreements strictly falls, proving transitivity. For freeness, define inside the proof a shortest simple-reflection expression for a nonidentity w and induct on its last factor, using signed simple-root coordinates to exhibit a positive root that w sends negative. Therefore no nonidentity element preserves the fundamental chamber.

items.title: Positive systems, bases, and chambers
items.statement: Positive systems and bases correspond bijectively to chambers, and W acts simply transitively on each set.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: A chamber assigns a constant sign to every root and hence a positive system; its indecomposable positives form the base. Conversely the inequalities of a base define that chamber. Apply simple transitivity.

items.title: Length and longest Weyl-group element
items.statement: For w∈W define its inversion set N(w)={α∈Φ⁺:w(α)∈Φ⁻} and its length by ℓ(w)=|N(w)|. A longest element is one maximizing this length; the next proposition identifies length with shortest simple-reflection word length and proves existence and uniqueness of the longest element.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Weyl length equals the positive-root inversion number
items.statement: For every w∈W, the shortest word length in the simple reflections equals ℓ(w)=|N(w)|. Consequently there is a unique longest element w₀, it satisfies w₀(Φ⁺)=Φ⁻, and ℓ(w₀)=|Φ⁺|.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

source_locators: Lecture 22, Weyl length and the longest element
items.strategy: First prove that a simple reflection s_i sends every positive root except alpha_i to a positive root. Comparing N(w) and N(ws_i) then changes the inversion count by exactly one, with the sign determined by w(alpha_i). The corresponding deletion/exchange argument shows that a simple-reflection word is shortest exactly along the count-increasing steps; induction gives ell(w)=|N(w)|. Simple transitivity supplies the unique element carrying the fundamental chamber to its opposite, hence carrying Phi⁺ to Phi⁻. Its inversion set is all of Phi⁺, so its length is |Phi⁺| and the inversion bound makes it longest.

items.title: Cartan matrix of a based root system
items.statement: For ordered simple roots α₁,…,α_r, the Cartan matrix has rows indexed by coroots: a_ij=(α_j,α_i∨)=2(α_j,α_i)/(α_i,α_i).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Finite-type Cartan-matrix properties
items.statement: A finite root-system Cartan matrix has a_ii=2, off-diagonal nonpositive integers, a_ij=0 iff a_ji=0, and is symmetrizable by positive diagonal entries so that the symmetrization is positive definite. Moreover a_ij a_ji∈{0,1,2,3}.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: The definitions give the diagonal and signs; symmetry of the inner product gives simultaneous zeros. Multiplication yields 4cos²θ and rank-two classification restricts it. Multiplying row i by (α_i,α_i)/2 recovers the positive-definite Gram matrix.

items.title: Dynkin diagram and arrow convention
items.statement: The Dynkin diagram has one vertex per simple root, a_ij a_ji edges between i,j, and for multiple edges an arrow pointing toward the shorter root. Isolated vertices are allowed.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: The Cartan matrix determines the based root system
items.statement: Two based finite root systems with the same Cartan matrix are isomorphic by the linear map carrying corresponding simple roots to one another.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: The matrix determines all simple-reflection matrices in the simple-root basis. The map between bases intertwines the generated Weyl groups. Every root is W-conjugate to a simple root (lower height by a simple reflection), so it carries Φ onto Φ′ and preserves Cartan integers.

items.title: Irreducibility and connected Dynkin diagrams
items.statement: A root system is irreducible exactly when its Dynkin diagram is connected.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Vertices in distinct connected components have zero inner product, so their spans split orthogonally. Conversely an orthogonal root-system split has no edges between its bases.

items.title: Finite irreducible Dynkin diagrams are controlled trees
items.statement: The underlying unoriented simple graph of a connected finite-type Dynkin diagram is a tree, has no vertex adjacent to more than three other vertices, and has at most one trivalent vertex. In the simply-laced trivalent case, if p≤q≤r are one plus the three arm lengths, then 1/p+1/q+1/r>1. If the diagram has a multiple edge, its underlying graph is a path and positivity permits only: a double edge at an end, a four-vertex path with its double edge in the middle, or a two-vertex triple edge.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Work only with the positive-definite symmetrized Gram matrix, without invoking the classification list. An explicit coefficient vector on a cycle has nonpositive quadratic value, so the graph is a tree; analogous vectors exclude degree four and two trivalent vertices. For a simply-laced trivalent tree, determinant recurrence along its three arms gives 1/p+1/q+1/r>1. For a path, the same recurrence together with edge products 1,2,3 shows that a triple edge forces two vertices, while a double edge is forced to an end except for the four-vertex path with a central double edge. A multiple edge attached to branching makes the relevant principal minor nonpositive. These exhaustive inequalities give precisely the stated graph restrictions before any type names are assigned.

items.title: Classification of irreducible reduced crystallographic root systems
items.statement: The irreducible reduced crystallographic root systems are exactly A_n (n≥1), B_n (n≥2), C_n (n≥3), D_n (n≥4), E₆,E₇,E₈,F₄,G₂, with B₁=C₁=A₁, B₂=C₂, D₂=A₁⊔A₁, and D₃=A₃.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: For a chain, determinant positivity and the rank-two edge products give A,B,C,F₄,G₂, with a multiple edge forced to an end except the four-vertex F₄ chain. For a simply-laced trivalent tree, order arm lengths p≤q≤r and apply 1/p+1/q+1/r>1: (2,2,r) gives D, (2,3,3),(2,3,4),(2,3,5) give E₆,E₇,E₈. The uniqueness theorem identifies types and direct inspection yields the low-rank coincidences.

items.title: Existence of every classified root system
items.statement: Every type in the classification is realized by a reduced crystallographic Euclidean root system with the indicated Dynkin diagram.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II
Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

source_locators: Knapp, Chapter II; Etingof, Lecture 23, Exercises 23.10 and 23.13
items.strategy: Construct A_n as {e_i-e_j} in the sum-zero space, B_n as {±e_i, ±e_i±e_j}, C_n as {±2e_i, ±e_i±e_j}, D_n as {±e_i±e_j}, and G2 in the hexagonal lattice. Construct F4 from ±e_i, ±e_i±e_j and the half-sums, and E8 from the D8 roots plus the even-sign half-sums; Etingof's exact polarization exercises certify the displayed F4 and E8 simple systems, while the item verifies the root-system axioms. Obtain E7 and E6 as explicit E8 subsystems and identify them by rank, root count, and the classification.

items.title: Duality of irreducible types
items.statement: Coroot duality exchanges B_n and C_n and fixes A_n,D_n,E₆,E₇,E₈,F₄,G₂ up to isomorphism.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Duality transposes the Cartan matrix and reverses every arrow. Inspecting the classified diagrams swaps B/C and leaves every other unoriented type isomorphic to its reversal.

items.title: Free Lie algebra on a vector space
items.statement: For a complex vector space V, the free Lie algebra L(V) is the Lie subalgebra generated by V inside the tensor algebra T(V) equipped with commutator bracket.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Universal property of the free Lie algebra
items.statement: Every linear map f:V→g to a complex Lie algebra extends uniquely to a Lie homomorphism L(V)→g.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Extend f uniquely to an associative-algebra homomorphism T(V)→U(g) and restrict to L(V); commutators map to Lie brackets. For uniqueness, the equalizer of two extensions is a Lie subalgebra containing V, hence all of L(V).

items.title: Lie algebra presented by generators and relations
items.statement: Given generators V and relations R⊂L(V), the presented Lie algebra is L(V)/I(R), where I(R) is the smallest Lie ideal containing R.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Serre Lie algebra of finite type
items.statement: For a finite-type Cartan matrix A=(a_ij), g(A) is generated by e_i,f_i,h_i with [h_i,h_j]=0, [h_i,e_j]=a_ij e_j, [h_i,f_j]=-a_ij f_j, [e_i,f_j]=δ_ij h_i, and (ad e_i)^{1-a_ij}e_j=(ad f_i)^{1-a_ij}f_j=0 for i≠j.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.title: Serre presentation theorem
items.statement: For every finite-type Cartan matrix A, the presented algebra g(A) is finite-dimensional semisimple, has Cartan subalgebra spanned by the h_i, root system with Cartan matrix A, and triangular decomposition n_-⊕h⊕n_+. Conversely a complex semisimple Lie algebra is generated by root sl₂ triples for its simple roots and has exactly these relations.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: First use PBW and the free-Lie universal property to obtain a triangular vector-space quotient. The adjoint triples act integrably: the Serre exponents are precisely the finite sl₂-string endpoints. Height induction shows every nonzero positive weight can be lowered by some f_i; the positive-definite root form then restricts possible weights to the finite root system Φ(A), proving finite dimensionality and one-dimensional real-root spaces. Pair opposite spaces by the invariant form constructed from the symmetrizer; its radical is an ideal meeting h trivially and height lowering makes it zero, so g(A) is semisimple. For a given semisimple g choose simple-root triples; root strings verify the relations and give a surjection g(A)→g. Both have h plus one-dimensional spaces indexed by the same Φ, so equal dimensions make it an isomorphism.

items.title: Isomorphism theorem for complex semisimple Lie algebras
items.statement: Two finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebras are isomorphic if their based root systems, equivalently their Cartan matrices, are isomorphic.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Choose corresponding bases and normalized root sl₂ triples. Serre’s theorem presents each algebra by the same generators and relations, and its universal maps are inverse on those generators.

items.title: Existence theorem for complex semisimple Lie algebras
items.statement: Every reduced crystallographic root system is isomorphic to the root system of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra; a nonempty irreducible root system yields a simple algebra, while the empty system yields the zero algebra.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Handle the empty system by the zero algebra. Otherwise choose component bases, apply the Serre construction to each component Cartan matrix, identify each resulting root system by its Cartan matrix, and take the direct sum.

items.title: Cartan–Killing classification of complex simple Lie algebras
items.statement: The finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebras are classified up to isomorphism by the connected Dynkin diagrams A_n,B_n,C_n,D_n,E₆,E₇,E₈,F₄,G₂ in the stated rank ranges.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

source_locators: Chapter II, Proposition 2.44, printed pp. 151–152, and §§10–11, printed pp. 196–202
items.strategy: A simple algebra has irreducible roots because an orthogonal root decomposition generates commuting nonzero ideals. Classification assigns one connected diagram. The isomorphism theorem gives uniqueness, and the existence theorem realizes every diagram by a simple algebra.

items.title: Classification of complex semisimple Lie algebras
items.statement: Finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebras are classified by finite disjoint unions of connected finite-type Dynkin diagrams, with multiplicity.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Decompose a semisimple algebra uniquely into simple ideals. Attach the connected diagram of each ideal; conversely take the direct sum of the simple algebras attached to the components.

items.title: The classical complex matrix Lie algebras sp and so
items.statement: Let n >= 1. The symplectic Lie algebra sp_{2n}(C) is the set of matrices A in M_{2n}(C) with A J_sp + J_sp A^T = 0, where J_sp = [[0, I_n], [-I_n, 0]]; the orthogonal Lie algebras so_{2n}(C) and so_{2n+1}(C) are the sets of A in M_m(C) with A J_so + J_so A^T = 0, where J_so = [[0, I_n], [I_n, 0]] for m = 2n and J_so = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, I_n], [0, I_n, 0]] for m = 2n + 1. Each set is closed under the commutator [A, B] = AB - BA, hence a Lie subalgebra of gl_m(C); in block form A = [[a, b], [c, -a^T]] with b, c symmetric for sp_{2n}(C) and skew-symmetric for so_{2n}(C), and A = [[0, u, w], [-w^T, a, b], [-u^T, c, -a^T]] with b, c skew-symmetric and u, w rows for so_{2n+1}(C).

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lecture 20.3, Examples 20.12-20.14, printed pp. 110-111

items.strategy: Solve A J + J A^T = 0 blockwise to obtain the displayed forms and their dimensions, then verify closure: if AJ = -JA^T and BJ = -JB^T, the four terms of [A,B]J + J[A,B]^T cancel in pairs. Each family is a nonzero proper subspace of M_m(C) closed under the commutator.

items.title: The classical complex matrix Lie algebras have split Cartan subalgebras
items.statement: In sp_{2n}(C), so_{2n}(C) and so_{2n+1}(C) the matrices whose a-part is a diagonal matrix diag(x_1, ..., x_n) and whose remaining blocks vanish (u = w = 0 in the odd orthogonal case) form a Cartan subalgebra h, isomorphic to C^n; h is a maximal toral subalgebra and equals its own centralizer in the ambient Lie algebra.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lecture 20.3, Examples 20.12-20.14, printed pp. 110-111

items.strategy: Compute [A, X] on each block to show that a matrix commuting with every diagonal a-part has a diagonal a-part and all off-diagonal blocks zero, so h is self-normalizing; the ad-image of h is simultaneously diagonalizable, so h is toral, and the block count gives dim h = n = rank. A Cartan subalgebra is a nilpotent self-normalizing subalgebra, and these two properties are checked directly.

items.title: Root systems of the classical complex Lie algebras
items.statement: With respect to the diagonal Cartan subalgebra h and the coordinate functionals e_i, assume n >= 2 for sl_n(C) and so_{2n}(C), and n >= 1 for sp_{2n}(C) and so_{2n+1}(C). The roots of sl_n(C) are the e_i - e_j with i != j; the roots of sp_{2n}(C) are the ±e_i ± e_j with i < j together with the ±2e_i; the roots of so_{2n}(C) are the ±e_i ± e_j with i < j; the roots of so_{2n+1}(C) are the ±e_i ± e_j with i < j together with the ±e_i. Each listed set is a reduced crystallographic Euclidean root system of type A_{n-1}, C_n, D_n, B_n respectively, subject to the standard low-rank identifications, and every root space is one-dimensional.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lecture 20.3, Examples 20.12-20.14, printed pp. 110-111

items.strategy: For each family take the matrix units adapted to the block form and compute [A, E_{ij}] = lambda(A) E_{ij} for A in h, reading off the a-, b-, c-, and (for the odd orthogonal case) u- and w-parts of the root set listed. The sets span R^n, their Cartan integers 2(a,b)/(a,a) are integers, the reflections s_a permute them, and the simple-root Cartan matrices are those of A_{n-1}, C_n, D_n, B_n.

items.title: Classical types correspond to sl, so, and sp
items.statement: The simple algebras of types A_n (n>=1), B_n (n>=2), C_n (n>=3), and D_n (n>=4) are sl_{n+1}(C), so_{2n+1}(C), sp_{2n}(C), and so_{2n}(C), with the stated low-rank coincidences handled separately.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Use the computed root systems and nondegenerate Killing forms in the stable simple ranges, apply the isomorphism theorem to the low-rank root coincidences, and prove so_4 is sl_2 plus sl_2 by the tensor-product construction.

items.title: Dimensions of exceptional simple Lie algebras
items.statement: The dimensions of G₂,F₄,E₆,E₇,E₈ are respectively 14,52,78,133,248.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Count roots in the explicit models: 12,48,72,126,240, then add ranks 2,4,6,7,8 using dim g=rank+|Φ|.

items.title: Dynkin diagrams do not classify global Lie groups
items.statement: A connected Dynkin diagram classifies a complex simple Lie algebra, and finite disjoint unions classify complex semisimple Lie algebras; neither classifies real forms or global connected Lie groups without additional data.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Lie Algebras, Algebraic Groups, and Lie Groups

items.title: Every finite reflection-invariant vector set is crystallographic
items.statement: False: reflection invariance alone does not force integral Cartan integers.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: Use the ten unit vectors at angles mπ/5. Reflection in the hyperplane perpendicular to any one of them preserves the angle set, while the Cartan integer 2cos(2π/5) is not integral.

items.title: Simple roots are pairwise orthogonal
items.statement: False: distinct simple roots have nonpositive, often nonzero, inner product.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: In A₂ the two simple roots meet at 120 degrees, so their inner product is negative.

items.title: Every connected finite graph is Dynkin
items.statement: False: positive definiteness and edge restrictions exclude most connected graphs.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: A cycle graph is connected but not a tree; its affine Cartan matrix has the all-ones vector in its kernel, contradicting positive definiteness.

items.title: Bₙ and Cₙ are always isomorphic
items.statement: False for n≥3: B_n and C_n are dual but not isomorphic as root systems.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

items.strategy: For n≥3 their oriented Dynkin diagrams reverse the unique double edge and are not isomorphic; only B₂=C₂ (and rank-one convention) coincide.

items.title: Dynkin diagrams classify real semisimple Lie algebras
items.statement: False: the diagram of the complexification does not distinguish real forms.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II
Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I

source_locators: Knapp Chapter II, §11, printed p. 203; Chapter VI
Etingof Lecture 20, real forms of sl_2
items.strategy: The nonisomorphic real algebras sl₂(R) and su(2), distinguished by Killing-form signature, have the same A₁ complexification.

items.title: The same Dynkin diagram forces isomorphic connected Lie groups
items.statement: False: a Lie algebra has distinct connected global forms.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, SU(2) and SO(3)
Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I

source_locators: Kirillov Exercises 2.8-2.10 and §3.10, printed pp. 24-25 and 44-45
items.strategy: Use the twofold cover SU(2) to SO(3), compute directly that su(2) complexifies to sl_2(C), and invoke the exact sl_2 root computation to identify the common A_1 diagram.

items.title: Classical root systems in coordinates
items.statement: For n>=2, A_{n-1}={ε_i−ε_j}, B_n={±ε_i}∪{±ε_i±ε_j}, C_n={±2ε_i}∪{±ε_i±ε_j} and D_n={±ε_i±ε_j} are reduced crystallographic root systems with the standard simple roots and Dynkin diagrams, and they are the root systems of the classical matrix Lie algebras.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II
Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19-24

source_locators: Chapter II, (2.43) and (2.50), printed pp. 150 and 155
items.strategy: Check finiteness, spanning, reducedness, reflection closure and integrality for the four displayed sets, then read off the standard Cartan matrices and match them with the matrix Lie algebras.

items.title: Weyl groups of B_n and D_n
items.statement: For n >= 1, W(B_n) is the full group of signed permutations of the coordinates, of order 2^n n!. For n >= 2, W(D_n) is the subgroup with an even number of sign changes, of order 2^{n−1} n!.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter II

source_locators: Chapter II, §6 and Problem 15, printed pp. 162-170 and 205
items.strategy: Read the reflections of B_n and D_n off the coordinate formulas, then count signed permutations with even sign change.

title: Root Systems Dynkin Diagrams and Cartan Killing Classification — Examples

items.title: The root system A₁
items.statement: The set {±α} in a Euclidean line is A₁; its Weyl group has order two and its Cartan matrix is [2].

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

source_locators: Knapp Chapter II, (2.43) and (2.50), printed pp. 150 and 155
items.strategy: Check the single reflection swaps the roots and compute the Cartan integer.

items.title: Rank-two systems A₂, B₂, and G₂
items.statement: Explicit planar 6-, 8-, and 12-root configurations realize A₂, B₂, and G₂ with Cartan products 1, 2, and 3.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Write explicit planar coordinates, apply each root reflection, and compute the two off-diagonal Cartan integers.

items.title: Simple roots and fundamental weights of Aₙ
items.statement: For A_n in the sum-zero subspace, α_i=e_i-e_{i+1} and ω_k=e_1+…+e_k-k/(n+1)Σe_i.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Pair ω_k with α_i∨=α_i and obtain δ_ki; positive roots are consecutive sums of the α_i.

items.title: The Weyl group of Aₙ is symmetric
items.statement: W(A_n) is S_{n+1}, acting by coordinate permutations.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Reflection in e_i-e_j swaps coordinates i,j; transpositions generate S_{n+1}, and every root reflection is such a swap.

items.title: Dynkin duality of Bₙ and Cₙ
items.statement: For n>=2, the B_n and C_n diagrams have the same chain and opposite double-edge arrows; transposing the Cartan matrix exchanges them.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Compute the final two simple-root lengths and Cartan entries in the coordinate models; the arrow points to the shorter root.

items.title: Low-rank Dynkin coincidences
items.statement: B₁=C₁=A₁, B₂=C₂, D₂=A₁⊔A₁, and D₃=A₃.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Identify the rank-one systems and B₂/C₂ by explicit similarities, then compute the D₂ decomposition and the D₃ Cartan graph from coordinate roots.

items.title: Serre relations for A₂ recover sl₃
items.statement: For A=[[2,-1],[-1,2]], the Serre generators map to E₁₂,E₂₃,E₂₁,E₃₂ and diagonal coroots in sl₃, yielding an isomorphism.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Check all defining brackets and all four quadratic Serre relations; the generated matrices span sl₃. Bound each Serre half by three dimensions and use the triangular decomposition plus surjectivity to prove injectivity.

items.title: Positive roots and highest root of G₂
items.statement: With α short and β long, the positive G₂ roots are α,β,α+β,2α+β,3α+β,3α+2β; the highest root is 3α+2β.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Generate roots by the two simple reflections, list the positive coordinate pairs, and compare them in the root order.

items.title: A cycle graph is not finite type
items.statement: The simply-laced cycle on m≥3 vertices has Cartan matrix 2I-adjacency, which is not positive definite.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: Evaluate the quadratic form on the all-ones vector: each vertex and edge contribution cancels, giving zero for a nonzero vector.

items.title: SL₂ and PGL₂ have the same Lie algebra but differ globally
items.statement: SL₂(C) and PGL₂(C) are connected Lie groups with Lie algebra sl₂(C) and Dynkin diagram A₁, but are not isomorphic.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, MIT 18.745 Lie Groups and Lie Algebras I, Lectures 19–24

items.strategy: The quotient map has kernel {±I}; SL₂ has nontrivial center while PGL₂ has trivial center, an isomorphism invariant.
